title: Globalization
objective: After this level you can explain how supply chains stretch across many countries.
summary: About half of world trade runs through global supply chains, like the iPhone 3G's. Globalization lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses piled up in particular places.

cards.headline: In March 2021, one stuck ship held up about $9 billion of trade a day.
cards.body: The Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal on March 23 and wasn't refloated until March 29. How could one ship matter so much? Because much of what you buy is pieced together across many countries.

cards.headline: Made in many places
cards.body: About half of global trade now happens inside global supply chains: networks that build products from parts and services sourced around the world. Take the iPhone 3G. Its parts came from firms in Japan, South Korea, Germany and the US. Then it was all assembled in China.

cards.fact: Assembly in China added $6.50 to an iPhone that cost $178.96 to make.
cards.context: That's about 3.6% of the total, by economists Yuqing Xing and Neal Detert's 2010 count. Yet trade statistics recorded all $178.96 as a Chinese export. Remember Level 73's trade balance, exports minus imports? With supply chains, the country on the label isn't always where most of the value was made.

mascot.line: "Made in China" turns out to mean "finished in China". Labels are short; supply chains are long.

cards.headline: Two sides of the same story
cards.body: Supporters point to prices and growth: globalization lets countries specialize, which lowers prices, and more open economies helped once extremely poor countries grow and cut poverty. Critics point to who paid. Economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found cheap Chinese imports had cost the US about 2.4 million jobs by 2011, concentrated in places that stayed worse off for years. Meanwhile, consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods. Both are true at once.

cards.headline: Globalization
learned: About half of trade runs through global supply chains
An iPhone 3G's parts came from four countries
Trade statistics can misplace where value is made
Lower prices and growth, but concentrated job losses

questions.prompt: What is a global supply chain?

options.label: A chain of shops selling one brand worldwide
options.rationale: Shops sell products; supply chains make them.

options.label: A network making products from parts sourced worldwide
A trade deal between two neighboring countries
options.rationale: A deal between two countries isn't a production network.

options.label: A shipping route through the Suez Canal
options.rationale: Shipping routes carry supply-chain goods, but aren't the chain itself.

questions.explanation: Global supply chains build products from parts and services sourced around the world, like the iPhone 3G.

questions.prompt: Why do critics of globalization point to particular towns rather than the whole US?

options.label: Import-driven job losses were concentrated there
Those towns paid higher prices for goods
options.rationale: Consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods, those towns included.

options.label: Only those towns traded with other countries
Those towns had no factories to begin with
options.rationale: The losses were in places that had factories and lost jobs.

questions.explanation: The China shock's job losses piled up in particular places, which stayed worse off, while consumers everywhere got slightly cheaper goods.

questions.prompt: From Level 73: an iPhone 3G assembled in China is shipped to the US. How much did trade statistics count as a Chinese export?

options.label: Nothing
options.rationale: It was counted as a Chinese export.
That's what Chinese assembly added, not what was recorded.

options.label: About half the cost
options.rationale: The whole value was recorded, not half.

questions.explanation: Trade statistics credited China with the full $178.96, though assembly there added only about $6.50.
